In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Why 1857 matters

The Revolt of 1857 was the first widespread challenge to East India Company rule. It began among Indian soldiers at Meerut and spread across north and central India, with leaders such as Rani Lakshmibai and Bahadur Shah Zafar. After it, power passed from the Company to the British Crown in 1858.

From petitions to mass movements

The Indian National Congress (1885) first sought reforms through petitions. The Partition of Bengal (1905) and the Swadeshi movement turned protest into action. Under Gandhi from 1919–20 it became a mass movement of non-cooperation, civil disobedience and finally Quit India in 1942.

The road to 1947

The Second World War weakened Britain, the INA trials and the naval mutiny of 1946 shook confidence in British control, and the Cabinet Mission and the Mountbatten Plan led to independence and partition on 15 August 1947. India became a republic on 26 January 1950.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Why the Constitution matters

The Constitution is the supreme law: it sets up the institutions of the state, divides powers between the Centre and the states, and guarantees rights to citizens. Every law must conform to it, and the Supreme Court can strike down laws that do not.

Rights, duties and directive principles

Fundamental Rights are enforceable in court. Directive Principles of State Policy guide the government but are not enforceable. Fundamental Duties (Article 51A), added in 1976, remind citizens of their obligations; there are 11 now, after the 86th Amendment added one in 2002.

How Parliament works

Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha (directly elected) and the Rajya Sabha (indirectly elected, a permanent house). A bill becomes law after both houses pass it and the President gives assent. Money bills originate only in the Lok Sabha.

8The basic structure doctrine

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Geography of India in brief

India is bounded by the Himalaya in the north, the Thar desert in the west, a long coastline (about 7,500 km including the islands) in the south and the Ganga–Brahmaputra plains in the north. The Ganga, Yamuna and Brahmaputra rise in the Himalaya; the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri are peninsular rivers.

Economic measures

GDP measures production, inflation measures price rises, the fiscal deficit measures the government's borrowing need, and per capita income measures average income. Together they describe the health of the economy. The Budget sets the government's income and spending plan for the year.

The role of institutions

The RBI manages money and credit, SEBI regulates the markets, NITI Aayog advises on policy, and the Finance Commission recommends how taxes are shared. GST is administered through the GST Council of the Centre and the states. Knowing which body does what answers many questions.

1Superlatives come in pairs

3Per capita divides by population

4Deficit = spending minus income

6Budget on 1 February, Survey a day earlier

Why it worksThe Survey sets the economic background for the Budget.

7Inflation and the repo rate

When inflation rises the RBI may raise the repo rate.

Why it worksHigher rates reduce borrowing and spending.

8Himalayan and peninsular rivers

Himalayan rivers are perennial; peninsular rivers are mostly seasonal.

Why it worksHimalayan rivers are fed by snow as well as rain.

9Deficit in one line

The ideas behind the topic, explained

What current affairs means for the exam

It means the events of roughly the last year that are likely to be asked: government schemes, appointments, summits, awards, sports results, economy and science. Exam setters choose facts with a definite answer (a name, a place, a date), so notes should capture exactly those.

A sustainable routine

Reading news daily without notes produces little. A better routine is 15 minutes a day to capture items in the 5 W template, 20 minutes a week to revise, and a monthly full recap. Consistency matters more than volume, and one reliable source avoids conflicting details.

How to verify a fact

Check names, dates and numbers against the official source (PIB, a ministry website, the organisation's own site). Be careful with 'first', 'largest' and 'highest' claims, which reports sometimes overstate. If two sources disagree, trust the official release.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Force changes motion

A force is any push or pull. A resultant force changes the speed or direction of a body; with no resultant force the velocity stays constant. This is the content of the first law, and the second law measures the change: more force gives more acceleration, more mass gives less.

Graph thinking

In a distance–time graph the slope is the speed. In a speed–time graph the slope is the acceleration and the area under the curve is the distance. A horizontal line in a distance–time graph means the body is at rest; in a speed–time graph it means constant speed.

Energy is conserved

Energy changes form but its total stays constant. A falling ball loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy of the same amount. In real situations some energy becomes heat, which is why mechanical energy appears to fall. The work done on a body equals its change in energy.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Light travels in straight lines

Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium, which explains shadows and the formation of images. At a surface it can be reflected (bounce back) or refracted (bend into the new medium). The law of reflection is exact: the angles of incidence and reflection are equal, measured from the normal.

Images in mirrors and lenses

A concave mirror and a convex lens converge light and can form real, inverted images or virtual, magnified ones depending on the object distance. A convex mirror and a concave lens diverge light and always give virtual, upright, reduced images. The sign convention keeps these results consistent.

Circuits in a nutshell

Current is the flow of charge, voltage is the push, and resistance opposes the flow. Ohm's law links them. In a series circuit one current passes through every part, so resistances add. In parallel, every branch has the same voltage and the current splits, so the reciprocals of resistance add.

1Use V = I × R in three forms

V = I × R, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I.

Why it worksThey are one formula rearranged, so remembering one gives all three.

2Series adds; parallel is smaller than the smallest

In parallel the total is always less than the smallest resistor.

Why it worksMore paths for the current means less total resistance.

3Convex mirrors and concave lenses always diverge

Why it worksA diverging system spreads the rays so they never meet in front.

4Sound needs a medium, light does not

Why it worksSound is a vibration of particles; light is an electromagnetic wave.

5Sound speed order: solid, liquid, gas

Why it worksCloser-packed particles pass the vibration along faster.

6Thunder after lightning

Light travels about a million times faster than sound.

Why it works3 × 10⁸ m/s compared with 343 m/s.

7Two equal resistors in parallel

The total is half of one: 4 Ω and 4 Ω give 2 Ω.

Why it worksTwo equal paths halve the resistance.

8The kilowatt-hour

1 kWh = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3.6 million joules.

Why it worksOne kilowatt-hour is one kilowatt used for one hour.

Thunder heard 3 s after lightning means the strike is about 1 km away.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

States and particles

The state of matter depends on how strongly the particles attract each other and how fast they move. In solids they vibrate in fixed positions, in liquids they slide past each other, in gases they move freely. Heating gives particles energy and can change the state; cooling does the reverse.

Pure substances and mixtures

Elements and compounds are pure substances with fixed properties. Mixtures vary in composition and keep the properties of their parts. Separation methods (filtration, evaporation, distillation, a magnet) rely on physical differences between the parts, which is the test for a mixture.

Reading the periodic table

Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number. Columns (groups) share the number of outer electrons and so have similar chemistry; rows (periods) show the shell being filled. Metals sit on the left and centre, non-metals on the right, and metalloids along the staircase.

1Element has one kind of atom; compound has a fixed ratio

Why it worksThe test is the number of different kinds of atom, not the number of atoms.

2The separation test for mixtures

If it can be separated by evaporation, filtering or a magnet, it is a mixture.

Why it worksPhysical separation works only when the substances are not chemically bonded.

3Neutrons = mass number − atomic number

5Sublimation skips the liquid

Camphor, dry ice and naphthalene go straight from solid to gas.

Why it worksTheir particles gain enough energy to escape without melting first.

6Moles = mass ÷ molar mass

36 g of water (18 g/mol) is 2 mol.

Why it worksMolar mass is the mass of one mole, so dividing counts the moles.

7Group number and valency

Group 1 elements have valency 1, group 2 valency 2, group 17 valency 1 (by gaining one electron).

Why it worksValency follows the outer-shell electrons.

8The density test

Density = mass ÷ volume; ice floats because its density is lower than water's.

Why it worksA less dense object floats on a denser liquid.

9Physical or chemical change

A change of state is physical; burning or rusting is chemical.

Why it worksA chemical change makes a new substance.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

What makes an acid an acid

In water, acids release hydrogen ions (H⁺) and bases release hydroxide ions (OH⁻). The more H⁺ a solution has, the lower its pH. Strength refers to how fully an acid or base ionises in water, which is different from concentration: strong acids ionise almost completely, weak acids only partly.

The logarithmic pH scale

pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration, so a one-unit change is a tenfold change. A solution at pH 3 has ten times more H⁺ than one at pH 4 and a hundred times more than one at pH 5. Neutral water has [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ and pH 7.

Salts and everyday chemistry

Neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base gives a neutral salt solution. Baking soda neutralises stomach acid in antacids, lime reduces soil acidity, and tooth decay is acid attacking enamel. Many exam facts are everyday examples of the same acid–base idea.

Why it worksRemember the pairs: Acid with Red, Base with Blue.

Why it worksIt changes colour only above about pH 8.3.

5Neutralisation always gives salt and water

Why it worksThe hydrogen of the acid and the hydroxide of the base join to make water, and the rest forms the salt.

6Acid + carbonate releases carbon dioxide

The fizzing shows that CO₂ is released.

Why it worksCarbonates break down in acid to release the gas, which turns lime water milky.

7Strong versus weak

HCl, H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ are strong acids; acetic and citric acids are weak.

Why it worksMineral acids ionise completely; organic acids only partly.

8Baking soda facts

NaHCO₃ is a mild base, and it releases CO₂ with an acid.

Why it worksIt reacts with acids to give carbon dioxide.

9Neutral salts

A strong acid with a strong base gives a neutral salt (pH 7).

Why it worksNeither ion changes the water's balance.

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Systems work together

Digestion breaks food into nutrients; the circulatory system carries them and oxygen to every cell; respiration releases energy; the excretory system removes waste; the nervous system coordinates everything. A failure in one system affects the others, which is why exam questions often link organs to functions across systems.

The heart and blood vessels

The heart pumps blood in a double circulation: the right side to the lungs, the left side to the body. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (usually oxygenated), veins carry it back (usually deoxygenated), and capillaries exchange materials with the tissues. Valves keep the blood flowing one way.

Nutrition and health

Carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins build tissue, vitamins and minerals protect and regulate. Lack of a particular vitamin or mineral causes a named deficiency disease. A balanced diet and hygiene prevent most such problems.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1Learn the digestive path as a story

Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum.

Why it worksFood moves in one direction, so the order is fixed and can be recited.

2The small intestine absorbs nutrients

Most nutrient absorption is in the small intestine; the large intestine absorbs mainly water.

Why it worksThe small intestine has villi, finger-like folds that give a huge surface area.

3Universal donor O negative, universal recipient AB positive

O negative has no A, B or Rh antigens, so no recipient reacts.

Why it worksReactions come from antigens, and O negative carries none.

4Pair each vitamin with one disease

C scurvy, D rickets, A night blindness, B1 beriberi.

Why it worksOne strong pairing is easier to recall than a list of symptoms.

5In the heart, the left ventricle has the thickest wall

The right side pumps blood to the lungs, the left side to the body.

Why it worksThe left ventricle must push blood round the whole body at high pressure.

6One verb per organ

Kidneys filter, lungs exchange, liver detoxifies.

Why it worksA single action word is enough for most 'which organ' questions.

7The pulmonary exception

The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

Why it worksVessels are named by direction relative to the heart, not by oxygen content.

8Enzymes in order

Saliva begins starch digestion in the mouth; pepsin acts on proteins in the stomach.

Why it worksEach region has its own enzymes.

9Hormone pairs

Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood sugar; thyroxine from the thyroid controls metabolism.

Why it worksOne gland, one headline hormone.

In depth

The ideas behind the topic, explained

Energy flows, matter cycles

Energy enters an ecosystem from the Sun, is captured by producers and passes along the food chain, losing about 90% at every step as heat. It cannot be recycled. Matter such as carbon, nitrogen and water, however, cycles repeatedly between living things and the environment.

Biodiversity and why it matters

Biodiversity provides food, medicine, clean air and water, and stability against disease and climate shocks. Loss of habitat, pollution, over-exploitation, invasive species and climate change are the main threats. Conservation protects habitats in the wild (in-situ) or breeds and stores species elsewhere (ex-situ).

Pollution and climate change

Air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide cause acid rain; greenhouse gases trap heat and raise global temperatures; CFCs thin the ozone layer. Water pollution from excess nutrients causes algal blooms and oxygen loss. Renewable energy, recycling and afforestation reduce these impacts.

The tricks

9 tricks, and why each one works

A trick you only memorise fails under pressure. Each one comes with its reason, so you can rebuild it if you forget it. Tap a trick to open it.

1The 10% rule

Each step up the food chain passes on about 10% of the energy.

Why it worksThe rest is lost as heat and used in life processes.

2A food chain always starts with a producer

Grass → Deer → Tiger.

Why it worksOnly producers capture the Sun's energy; everything else depends on them.

3Biodiversity has three levels

Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.

Why it worksVariety can be measured within a species, between species and between ecosystems.

4In-situ is 'in place'; ex-situ is 'out of place'

A national park is in-situ; a zoo is ex-situ.

Why it worksThe Latin words mean in position and out of position.

5CFCs destroy ozone; CO₂ and CH₄ warm the Earth

These are two different problems.

Why it worksOzone loss lets in UV rays; greenhouse gases trap heat.

6Biomagnification is highest at the top

Top predators carry the most toxin.

Why it worksToxins are not broken down, so they build up at each level.

7The carbon cycle

Plants take in CO₂; animals, fire and decay release it.

Why it worksPhotosynthesis and respiration are opposite processes.

8Energy pyramids are always upright

A pyramid of energy can never be inverted.

Why it worksEnergy decreases at every step.

9Biodiversity hotspots

India has hotspots in the Himalaya, Indo-Burma and the Western Ghats.

Why it worksHotspots are species-rich and threatened.
